title: Area IX review: Emergency Operations
intro: These questions mix the four single-engine Tasks of Area IX: emergency descent, emergency approach and landing, systems and equipment malfunctions, and emergency equipment and survival gear. Many of them join two Tasks in one flight, because a malfunction often leads to a descent, a landing, and then the wait for rescue.

questions.q: The examiner gives you an emergency descent and asks you to level off at 4,500 ft. You are coming down at about 2,500 fpm. Using the AFH's 10 percent level-off lead as a starting point, where do you begin the level-off, and what altitude range meets the ACS?
options: Begin near 4,600 ft; end between 4,400 and 4,600 ft
Begin near 4,750 ft; end between 4,450 and 4,550 ft
Begin near 4,525 ft; end between 4,350 and 4,650 ft
Begin near 4,750 ft; end between 4,400 and 4,600 ft
questions.why: The AFH gives its level-off lead as 10 percent of the descent rate above the target, 100 ft for a 1,000 fpm descent (its example is a partial-power descent) [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]. It names no special lead for an emergency descent, so treat 10 percent as a starting point: 10 percent of 2,500 fpm is 250 ft, and 4,500 + 250 = 4,750 ft. The ACS wants the level-off at the specified altitude within 100 ft, so 4,400 to 4,600 ft (ACS CA.IX.A.S5). Starting at 4,600 ft copies the 100 ft lead from a 1,000 fpm descent and will likely overshoot at 2,500 fpm.

questions.q: On one checkride flight the examiner asks for an emergency descent with a target of 120 KIAS. Later the examiner closes the throttle for a simulated engine failure, and your POH best glide is 70 KIAS. Which pair of airspeeds meets both commercial ACS standards?
options: 121 KIAS in the descent, 70 KIAS in the glide
112 KIAS in the descent, 79 KIAS in the glide
115 KIAS in the descent, 58 KIAS in the glide
109 KIAS in the descent, 75 KIAS in the glide
questions.why: The emergency descent tolerance is +0/-10 knots, so 110 to 120 KIAS (ACS CA.IX.A.S5). The best glide tolerance is plus or minus 10 knots, so 60 to 80 KIAS (ACS CA.IX.B.S1). 112 and 79 are both inside. 121 KIAS fails even by 1 knot, because +0 means no overshoot; 109 is 1 knot under the floor; 58 is below 60. The descent limit is a ceiling because going faster can pass structural limits such as VNE, VLE or VFE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

questions.q: Practicing emergency descents with your CFI in a piston single, you hold idle and high speed from 8,500 ft down to 3,000 ft before you recover. Your CFI says you held it far too long. What reason does the AFH give for ending a practice descent once it is established and stable?
options: The ACS limits the descent to 1,000 ft of altitude loss
A long descent at idle uses up too much of the fuel reserve
Prolonged practice can cool the engine cylinders too much
Holding the bank that long makes the load factor build up
questions.why: In training, once the descent is established and stabilized it should be ended, and prolonged practice in piston airplanes should be avoided to prevent excessive cooling of the cylinders [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]. High-speed descents give the engine excess cooling air and can shock cool it with abrupt temperature changes [[1:177|PHAK 7-17]]. The ACS sets no altitude-loss limit; it asks for the bank, airspeed and level-off standards (ACS CA.IX.A.S4, S5). A steady 30 to 45 degree bank does not keep adding load factor.

questions.q: Smoke is coming from under the panel. You are two minutes into a steady descending turn when you bend down and sideways to pull the fire extinguisher from under your seat. As you sit up you feel a strong tumbling sensation. What is it, and what helps?
options: The leans; roll the wings level to match the feeling
Somatogravic illusion; lower the nose to cancel the pitch-up feeling
Coriolis illusion; trust the attitude indicator and keep head movement small
Early hypoxia from the smoke; descend faster before doing anything else
questions.why: After a turn long enough for the inner-ear fluid to move with the canal, a head movement in another plane can create a strong false sense of turning on a different axis. The PHAK says to retrieve objects with minimal head movement and be alert for it [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. That is the Coriolis illusion, and the attitude indicator tells the truth. The leans come from rolling out after a long turn, not from a head movement. Fly the airplane first; use the extinguisher, then ventilate [[24:359|AFH 18-10]], and know its location and operation from your preflight briefing [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]].

questions.q: In a real emergency descent for cabin smoke, you see a low-wing airplane ahead and below, crossing your path. It shows no sign of seeing you. Which statement is right?
options: You have the right-of-way as an aircraft in distress, so hold your path; it must give way
You have the right-of-way as an aircraft in distress, but you must still see and avoid, so steer clear of it
It has the right-of-way, because aircraft converging from the right have priority
Right-of-way rules no longer apply, because 14 CFR 91.3 lets you deviate in an emergency
questions.why: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(c)]]. But every pilot, IFR or VFR, must stay vigilant to see and avoid other aircraft when weather permits [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]], and the other pilot can give way only if he sees you. That is why the descent is flown in a turn to check for traffic below [[24:357|AFH 18-8]]. 91.3 allows deviation only to the extent needed to meet the emergency [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]; it does not make collision avoidance optional.

questions.q: Your engine quits at 5,000 ft over open ocean. No shore, boat or ship is within any glide. You want as much time as possible to send a MAYDAY, actuate the ELT and get the passengers into their vests before you set up for the ditching. Which speed fits that goal?
options: Minimum sink, generally a few knots below best glide
Best glide, because it gives the most distance
Maneuvering speed, to protect the structure on impact
The slowest speed you can hold above the stall horn
questions.why: Minimum sink speed gives the lowest rate of descent and the most time in the air, at the cost of distance. The AFH names ditching at sea as an example of when time matters more than distance, and says it is generally a few knots below best glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]]. Best glide buys distance, which helps only when there is somewhere to reach, such as a surface vessel to ditch near [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Flying at the edge of the stall gives neither more time nor safety.

questions.q: Carburetor heat and the restart items did not cure a rough engine. It still makes some power, and you are committed to a long field 2 miles ahead. What does the AFH recommend about that power?
options: Shut the engine down now, because a rough engine is a fire risk
Keep it running through touchdown so you can go around if needed
Use the power it gives, then switch the engine and fuel off just before touchdown
Keep cycling the mixture and magnetos until it runs smoothly again
questions.why: The AFH says to exploit the power from an irregularly running engine, but it is generally better to switch the engine and fuel off just before touchdown. That keeps you in charge of the situation, and a cooled-down engine greatly lowers the fire hazard [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Power is what makes a precautionary landing less hazardous than a forced one, because it lets you correct errors [[24:350|AFH 18-1]], so shutting down early throws that away. Endless troubleshooting at the expense of flying is a classic trap [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

questions.q: On short final to your forced-landing field, at about 150 ft AGL, a gusty crosswind is pushing you off your line. You suddenly remember that the doors are still latched and the fuel selector is still on. What comes first?
options: Hold attitude, airspeed and alignment; checklist items wait while control needs you
Unlatch the doors and shut off the fuel now, since they matter most after touchdown
Lower full flaps now to slow down before you deal with the checklist
Turn away to buy time to finish the checklist, then line up again
questions.why: Positive control of the airplane during the final part of the approach has priority over everything else, including configuration and checklist tasks [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Losing control of attitude and sink rate at touchdown is called the most critical error in an emergency landing [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Doing the items with your head down while the gusts move you is how the field is lost. Turning away low brings steep banks near the ground, which raise the stall speed and risk a wingtip strike [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

questions.q: You are planning a for-hire survey flight over a mix of forest and farmland. According to the AFH, which three things govern your choice of emergency landing sites if the engine quits?
options: Wind direction and speed, field size and slope, and obstacles on final
Fuel on board, gross weight and density altitude
Time of day, distance to the nearest airport, and how many people are on board
The route chosen in preflight planning, your height above the ground, and any excess airspeed
questions.why: The AFH lists the route selected in preflight planning, the height above the ground when the emergency happens, and excess airspeed, which can be turned into distance or altitude [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Wind, field size and slope, and obstacles on final are the three factors for planning the approach once you have a field, not for choosing one [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. Planning is the first step: except for takeoff and landing, fly at an altitude that allows an emergency landing without undue hazard to persons or property on the surface [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119(a)]].

questions.q: Your engine fails at 3,000 ft AGL. You pick field A, but at 2,000 ft you see wires across it and switch to field B, a long, open pasture well within reach. At 800 ft you notice field C, a little smoother, off to one side and reachable only with a steep turn. What should you do?
options: Switch to C, because it is the better surface
Stay with B; you have changed once, and C is not needed to avoid disaster
Pick whichever of B or C is closer to a road
Go back to A, since you first chose it with the most altitude
questions.why: As a rule, do not change your mind more than once: a well-flown crash landing in poor terrain can be less hazardous than an uncontrolled touchdown on a good field [[24:353|AFH 18-4]]. A late switch makes sense only when the chosen field would obviously end in disaster and a better one is within gliding distance, and last-minute changes bring hazards such as excessive maneuvering at very low altitude [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. B is a sound field, and a steep turn at 800 ft raises the stall speed [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].

questions.q: Your engine quits and the only usable field is long and clear at both ends, with a 16-knot wind along it. You expect to touch down at 48 KIAS. Which choice and reason fit the AFH?
options: Land into the wind: your groundspeed is 32 knots against 64 downwind, so a downwind touchdown carries four times the destructive energy
Land downwind, because a tailwind carries you farther and that matters more than touchdown speed
Either way, because the airspeed is the same, so the crash forces are the same
Land into the wind, because a downwind touchdown carries twice the destructive energy
questions.why: Groundspeed is the most critical part of crash severity: doubling it quadruples the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]]. Into the wind, 48 - 16 = 32 knots; downwind, 48 + 16 = 64 knots. That is double the groundspeed, so 2 x 2 = 4 times the energy. A tailwind does stretch a glide [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], but that only helps you reach the field; once you are there, the AFH wants the lowest possible groundspeed at touchdown. Twice the energy treats energy as growing in step with speed, which is the wrong rule.

questions.q: You forgot pitot heat in visible moisture near freezing. Now smoke forces an emergency descent. Nose low at idle, wind noise rising, the airspeed reads lower and lower as you descend, and during a brief level-off it did not change even when you added power. What is the best explanation and response?
options: The pitot tube is blocked but the drain hole is open, so you really are slowing down; lower the nose more
The pitot tube and its drain hole are blocked, so the needle responds to altitude, not speed; your real speed may be near the limits, so fly attitude and power and slow down
The static port is blocked, and a blocked static port always reads low; ignore it and continue
Nothing is wrong; the gear and propeller drag are slowing the airplane as planned
questions.why: With both the pitot tube and drain hole blocked, the trapped pressure makes the airspeed stop responding to speed changes and change only with altitude, reading lower in a descent [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. With the drain open the reading would drop to zero quickly [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]], and a blocked static port reads high, not low, as you descend below the blockage [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. In an emergency descent the danger is real overspeed, since you must not pass VNE, VLE or VFE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]] (application: use pitch attitude, power and sound as the speed cues, and turn the pitot heat on).

questions.q: Cruising on a humid 15 C day in a carbureted airplane with a constant-speed propeller, you notice the manifold pressure has crept from 23 down to 21 inches. Rpm is steady at 2,400. What is most likely, and what do you do?
options: Carburetor ice; apply full carburetor heat and leave it on until normal power returns
No ice, because carburetor ice always shows first as an rpm drop
A governor fault; pull the propeller control back to raise the manifold pressure
Carburetor ice; apply partial heat to save power and avoid roughness
questions.why: With a constant-speed propeller the governor holds rpm, so carburetor ice usually shows as a drop in manifold pressure with no drop in rpm; the rpm drop is the fixed-pitch sign [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. The fix is full heat, left on until normal power returns, since partial heat or too short a time can make icing worse [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. With ice present, expect manifold pressure to drop at first and then rise slowly as the ice melts [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

questions.q: In hazy cruise the attitude indicator slowly shows a 10 degree left bank, and the heading indicator is slowly turning. The electric turn coordinator shows wings level, the magnetic compass heading is steady, the VSI shows zero and the altimeter is steady. What is the best response?
options: The turn coordinator has failed, so follow the attitude indicator
The static system has failed, so open the alternate static source
Roll right to level the attitude indicator, then compare the instruments again
Suspect a vacuum failure; check the suction gauge, fly on the turn coordinator, VSI and altimeter, and cover the failed gyros
questions.why: A quick comparison of the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI checks the vacuum, electrical and static systems against each other [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Here the two vacuum gyros disagree with the electric and static instruments, which fits a failing vacuum source whose gyros slow and wander [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Most airplanes power the turn coordinator electrically so one failure still leaves bank information [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Covering the failed instruments helps, and then tell ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Rolling to match the bad gyro would put you in a real bank.

questions.q: Ice has blocked the static ports of your unpressurized airplane, which has no alternate static source. The altimeter is frozen. What does the IFH say you could do?
options: Break the glass of the airspeed indicator to let static air in
Rely on the VSI, since it has its own static line
Break the glass of the VSI, accepting some extra instrument error
Nothing; without an alternate source the altimeter cannot be restored
questions.why: A static problem affects the airspeed indicator, the altimeter and the VSI together. With no alternate static source in an unpressurized airplane, the pilot could break the VSI glass: the VSI is not required for instrument flight, and this gives the altimeter and airspeed indicator a static source, though it may add errors [[23:333|IFH 11-8]]. The VSI shares the blocked static system, so it is no help on its own. Breaking the airspeed glass would ruin the instrument you need.

questions.q: Your alternator failed 25 minutes ago and the battery is weak. Your flaps are electric. Your POH shows a 1,350 ft landing distance with full flaps. Which is the shortest of these runways that still covers the AFH's worst case for a no-flap landing, an increase of as much as 50 percent?
questions.why: Flap and gear motors draw far more current than other equipment, and selecting them on a partly depleted battery may cause an immediate total electrical loss, so plan a no-flap landing [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. A no-flap landing needs substantially more runway, and the increase could be as much as 50 percent [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]: 1,350 x 1.5 = 2,025 ft. 2,100 ft is the shortest option that covers it. 1,900 ft covers only about a 41 percent increase, and 1,500 ft only 11 percent. 2,700 ft is long enough but is not the shortest.

questions.q: Passing 400 ft after takeoff, the passenger door bangs open and the noise is loud. Your passenger shouts to get back on the ground right away. What does the AFH recommend?
options: Make a steep turn back to the runway at once
Loosen your harness and reach across to pull the door shut
Keep flying: climb to pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern and make a normal landing
Land straight ahead, since the airplane may not keep flying
questions.why: If a door opens after liftoff, do not rush to land: climb to normal pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern and land normally, completing the landing checklist. Rushing can lead to steep turns at low altitude, and an open door seldom affects a light single's ability to fly [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Do not release the seat belt and harness to reach it; close it on the ground [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Open-door accidents come from distraction and loss of control, not the door [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

questions.q: The up-elevator cable breaks. Using trim and power you make a gentle landing in a hayfield. No one is hurt and the airplane is not damaged. What do the NTSB rules require?
options: Notify the nearest NTSB office immediately, because a flight control system failure is a listed serious incident
Nothing, because without injury or substantial damage it is not an accident
Only a written report to the FAA, if the FAA asks for one under 14 CFR 91.3
Notify the NTSB within 10 days, since nobody was hurt
questions.why: An accident needs death, serious injury or substantial damage [[60:881|49 CFR 830.2]], so this was not one. But 830.5 also requires the operator to notify the nearest NTSB office immediately for listed serious incidents, and the first on the list is a flight control system malfunction or failure [[60:882|49 CFR 830.5]]. The 91.3 written report is a separate FAA matter for deviating from a rule [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]; it does not replace the NTSB notice.

questions.q: Your ELT is inoperative at a remote strip where it cannot be repaired. You plan to ferry the airplane to a shop 120 NM away under 14 CFR 91.207(e). The owner wants to ride along. May he?
options: Yes, if you placard the airplane 'ELT not installed'
No, only required crewmembers may be aboard a ferry flight under 91.207(e)
Only if the flight stays within 50 NM of the departure airport
Yes, because ferry flights have no limit on who is aboard
questions.why: 91.207(e) lets you ferry an airplane with an inoperative ELT from a place where repairs cannot be made to a place where they can, but no one other than required crewmembers may be carried [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(e)]]. The placard goes with a different exception, for an ELT removed for repair up to 90 days, and the 50 NM exception is for training flights only [[60:490|14 CFR 91.207(f)]].

questions.q: Cruising with 121.5 MHz on your second radio, you hear an ELT tone that grows louder and then fades. What does the AIM ask you to report to the nearest air traffic facility?
options: Nothing until you have circled down low and found the wreck yourself
Only the position where the signal was strongest, since that is where the wreck is
Nothing, because satellites already track every ELT
Your positions when you first heard it, last heard it and heard it strongest, with your altitudes and the frequency
questions.why: The AIM asks for your position when the signal was first heard, when it was last heard and at maximum strength, plus your altitudes and the frequency, 121.5 or 243.0 MHz, with positions relative to a navaid if you can [[34:32|AIM 6-2-4]]. Satellite monitoring of 121.5 and 243.0 MHz stopped in 2009, so a 121.5 signal depends on someone hearing and reporting it [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]].

questions.q: You have become incapacitated and your passenger activated Emergency Autoland. The airplane is flying straight and level past several airports without turning toward any of them. The display shows that GPS is lost. What is happening?
options: It keeps flying straight and will not try to land until GPS coverage returns
It is following ATC vectors that the passenger cannot hear
It is heading for the nearest airport with an ILS, which may be far away
It has finished its descent and now waits for a pilot to take over
questions.why: If the EAL system loses GPS coverage, the airplane continues straight flight without trying to land until GPS returns [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. It picks airports only among those with an RNAV or GPS approach, by weather, wind, runway length and towered status [[24:371|AFH 18-22]]. It does not take ATC instructions [[24:372|AFH 18-23]], so it is not following vectors.

questions.q: You plan three 90-minute legs over sparsely settled country and want the best search and rescue protection if you have to make a forced landing on the way. What does the AIM recommend?
options: One VFR flight plan with all the stops, since a search starts 30 minutes after each stop's ETA
File only to your first landing, and refile for each leg
No flight plan is needed if the airplane has a 121.5 MHz ELT
One flight plan, with a single ETE to the final destination
questions.why: For maximum protection, file only to the point of first intended landing and refile for each leg. With one long plan, a mishap on any leg probably would not start a search until 30 minutes after your ETA at the final destination [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]]. A 121.5 ELT is not watched by satellites and depends on someone hearing it [[34:30|AIM 6-2-4]]. This matters because an injured survivor's life expectancy can drop as much as 80 percent in the first 24 hours [[34:34|AIM 6-2-6]].

questions.q: After a forced landing in remote terrain, one passenger has a badly broken leg. You hear a search airplane in the distance. Which ground signal from the AIM survivor code fits best, and how should you lay it out?
options: A V, as small and neat as possible so it reads clearly
A Y, at least 3 ft high, next to the airplane
An N, laid in dark material on dark ground
An X, at least 10 ft high, with strong color contrast
questions.why: In the AIM ground-air visual code, X means require medical assistance and V means require assistance; X fits an injured passenger. Symbols should be at least 10 ft high, with as much color contrast as possible, and the pilot overhead acknowledges by rocking the wings [[34:36|AIM FIG 6-2-1]]. V is tempting but asks only for general help. Stay with the airplane unless you have good reason to think you will not be found [[34:47|AIM 6-3-2]].

questions.q: After a forced landing, a fuel line broke and sprayed fuel into a passenger's eyes. You are well away from the airplane and have clean water. What does the PHAK say to do?
options: Do nothing until rescuers arrive, since water can spread the fuel
Flush the eyes briefly, then seek medical attention only if irritation continues
Wipe the eyes with a cloth and keep them closed until help arrives
Flush the eyes immediately with clean water for at least 15 minutes and get medical attention immediately
questions.why: For fuel in the eyes, the PHAK says to flush immediately with clean water for at least 15 minutes and seek medical attention immediately [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. 'Seek medical attention if irritation occurs' is the PHAK advice for engine oil in the eyes, not fuel [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. Fuel is the more serious exposure, so do not wait to see.

questions.q: Over water, you are cruising at 4,500 ft with a glide ratio of about 10 to 1. A strong headwind means your fuel will run out about 15 NM before the coast. A fishing boat is below you. What do the AIM and AFH support?
options: Press on and glide the last miles, since a few gallons may be left in the tanks
Go to idle now and glide toward the coast to save the fuel
Ditch near the boat while you still have power, after a MAYDAY and the ELT
Wait until the tanks are dry so the empty tanks help the airplane float
questions.why: A 10 to 1 glide means 10 ft forward for each foot of altitude [[24:82|AFH 3-21]]: from 4,500 ft that is 45,000 ft, about 7.4 NM (6,076 ft per NM), so you cannot glide the 15 NM that remain. When it is certain the coast cannot be reached, ditch before the fuel is exhausted if possible, because power matters so much in a ditching [[34:51|AIM 6-3-3]]. Make every effort to ditch near a surface vessel, and actuate your ELT if the installation permits [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. A precautionary landing with power is generally less hazardous than a forced landing, and pressing on with wishful thinking is what turns one into the other [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].
